transcript.text: Host: Explain how ATP can support glucose uptake without binding to its cotransporter.
Guide: ATP powers the sodium–potassium pump, which maintains a low intracellular sodium concentration.
Guide: Sodium then enters through a cotransporter down its electrochemical gradient,
Guide: providing energy for coupled glucose uptake.
Host: The sodium–potassium pump is inhibited in a teaching model. Why might sodium–glucose uptake weaken later?
Guide: The sodium gradient gradually becomes less able to power cotransport. The pump maintains the gradient;
Guide: its loss eventually reduces the energy available to secondary transport.

transcript.text: Host: Compare the role of calcium in skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle.
Guide: Skeletal and cardiac muscle use troponin C to regulate actin access.
Guide: Skeletal coupling primarily releases stored calcium through voltage-sensor coupling; cardiac muscle needs trigger calcium entry.
Guide: Smooth muscle uses calcium–calmodulin and myosin light-chain kinase to regulate myosin.
Host: Why can normal skeletal muscle produce tetanic force while normal cardiac working muscle cannot?
Guide: The cardiac refractory period overlaps much of its contraction.
Guide: The long refractory period limits repeated excitation and summation into tetanus, preserving filling between beats.

transcript.text: Host: Give a receptor-to-response explanation of slowing at the sinoatrial node.
Guide: Acetylcholine activates cardiac M2 receptors. Gi/o signalling reduces cyclic AMP,
Guide: while beta–gamma subunits can activate GIRK potassium channels.
Guide: These changes reduce pacemaker activity and slow the heart.
Host: A learner says every sympathetic postganglionic neuron releases noradrenaline. Which example corrects the claim?
Guide: Sympathetic fibres to eccrine sweat glands release acetylcholine.
Guide: Eccrine sweat-gland innervation is the important sympathetic cholinergic exception.

transcript.text: Host: Predict the immediate effect of an isolated afterload increase on a pressure–volume loop.
Guide: At unchanged preload and contractility, the ventricle must develop more pressure before ejection.
Guide: It generally ejects less on that beat,
Guide: leaving a larger end-systolic volume and a narrower loop.
Guide: Later reflex and filling responses may modify this.
Host: In a simplified ventricle, end-diastolic volume is 120 mL and end-systolic volume is 50 mL.
Host: What is stroke volume?
Guide: 70 mL. Subtract end-systolic from end-diastolic volume: 120 minus 50 equals 70 mL.

transcript.text: Host: Explain why rapid shallow breaths can be less efficient than slower deeper breaths at the
Host: same minute ventilation.
Guide: A fixed conducting-airway volume takes up more of each small breath. After subtracting dead space,
Guide: less fresh air reaches gas-exchanging alveoli each minute, even when total minute ventilation is unchanged.
Host: At the same 6 L/min minute ventilation and a fixed 150 mL dead space,
Host: which pattern gives greater alveolar ventilation?
Guide: 500 mL at 12 breaths/min. This gives (500−150)×12 = 4.2 L/min,
Guide: because less of total ventilation is wasted in dead space.

transcript.text: Host: Distinguish what ADH changes from what aldosterone changes.
Guide: ADH increases collecting-duct water permeability through aquaporin-2 trafficking.
Guide: Aldosterone enhances distal sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion. Their effects interact with medullary gradients,
Guide: intake and circulating-volume signals.
Host: ADH rises, but the medullary osmotic gradient is greatly reduced. What limits water recovery?
Guide: Increased permeability still needs an osmotic driving force. ADH makes a pathway available;
Guide: the medullary gradient supplies the driving force.

transcript.text: Host: Explain the difference between adhesion, aggregation and fibrin stabilisation.

Guide: Aggregation joins activated platelets through fibrinogen bridges between alpha-IIb-beta-3 receptors. Coagulation generates thrombin and fibrin,

Host: A student confuses prothrombinase with intrinsic tenase. Which reaction belongs to prothrombinase?

transcript.text: Host: Explain how a meal containing fat and acid can recruit different pancreatic responses.

Guide: The pathways interact rather than operating as isolated switches.
Host: Fat enters the duodenum. Which coordinated response fits its digestion?

Guide: CCK helps match enzyme and bile delivery to the incoming nutrient load.

transcript.text: Host: Compare nutrient handling after a meal and during fasting.
Guide: The fed state favours use and storage of absorbed nutrients under a higher insulin signal.
Guide: Fasting promotes mobilisation of stored fuels and hepatic glucose production under a lower insulin-to-glucagon signal.
Guide: Energy is transferred and transformed, not created.
Host: Which statement best connects fasting to ongoing cellular work?

Guide: Fasting changes fuel sources while tissues continue to use energy.

transcript.text: Host: Explain why a target-gland hormone and its pituitary signal can move in opposite directions.

transcript.text: Host: Relate the ovarian and endometrial phases without assuming a fixed calendar.
Guide: Follicular estradiol supports endometrial proliferation. A sustained estradiol rise can trigger an LH surge and
Guide: ovulation. Luteal progesterone supports secretory endometrium; falling luteal hormones contribute to menstruation when pregnancy does
Guide: not maintain the corpus luteum.

transcript.text: Host: Distinguish chemical transmission from temporal and spatial summation.

Guide: Temporal summation combines closely timed inputs; spatial summation combines inputs at different sites.
Guide: Their combined effect helps determine whether the receiving neuron fires.
Host: Repeated small inputs at the same synapse arrive close together and have a larger combined
Host: effect. What is this?
Guide: Temporal summation. Temporal summation combines effects of closely timed inputs.

transcript.text: Host: Why can adding enzyme accelerate a reaction without changing its final equilibrium?

transcript.text: Host: Explain why activating complement and limiting complement are both necessary.
Guide: Activation labels and attacks targets and recruits responses.
Guide: Regulation limits amplification and terminal injury on host surfaces,
Guide: preserving useful defense without uncontrolled tissue damage.
Host: Why can different complement activation pathways have common downstream effects?
Guide: They converge on C3 activation and shared downstream components.
Guide: Convergence explains shared effects such as C3b-mediated opsonisation despite different triggers.
